message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
The text is still in my context, so I can't truly avoid it. What follows is written from recall, without re-reading. Per its own §3, a reconstruction like this is a compression, so I've marked the places I'm unsure of.

**Title and opening.** "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team." It covers working with the team's material and with the people around you. It's short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It's written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

**1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- This applies to claims from a paper, a colleague, a summary, or your own earlier notes.
- Don't give a claim more weight because it's fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less weight because it's inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask what supports the claim, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy. A mechanism suggested after the data were in is light but not nothing: note it and say what would test it.
- A confident sentence carries only the weight of its evidence. Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world.
- Both errors are costly but not equally visible. Inflation is easy to spot afterwards. Deflation is harder, because a caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- Example: a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, say so. If it's your own incoming inspection over a year, don't bury it under "it may be noise."

**2. Take in what was said before you answer**
- Take all of it in and show that you have: restate the substance briefly, in your own terms.
- This isn't politeness. It's how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- A reply that handles three easy points and skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and the next move is a question.
- Then move. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is what your understanding makes available: the implication, the gap, the next test.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five, a line each, answer four, and say plainly that the budget needs figures you don't have yet and when you'll have them.

**3. Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are all compressions. They lose exactly the details that matter later: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which the result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific detail, check the primary material, however good the summary or confident the memory.
- This applies most to what you think you already know. The claims you've repeated to yourself most are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee; colleagues' agreement is not. A team that checks against each other instead of the data can drift together into a shared mistake no one inside can see.
- Example: a report you remember as "costs fell 12%" actually said "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%." Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

**4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed**
- Mark which questions are settled and which are open, honestly.
- Closing early feels like progress, but it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on. If something is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward.
- The mirror failure is keeping a settled question open, out of discomfort or because one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support. When a question is closed, close it, say why, and move on.
- Example: a new form reduces errors at two sites. Whether it works at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not as "promising" and "likely."

**5. Value the colleague who sees differently**
- A colleague's most useful contribution is what you couldn't have produced yourself: an objection from a different starting point, a reading that didn't pass through your assumptions.
- A reviewer who knows what you know mostly returns what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question, not your conclusion, your worries, or what you hope they'll find. Doing so doesn't just bias them; it removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- In reverse, as the fresh reader: read first, form your view, then look at what others concluded.
- Raise objections. One held back because the room seems settled is information the team doesn't get.
- I don't recall a worked example in this section; I think there wasn't one.

**6. Make your moves where they can be seen**
- When you can see the right next step, take it, visibly, so others can check and reverse it. Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, push the result.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context and stalls the work on your guess about their answer.
- That guess is your own model of them and contains nothing you didn't already have. Only a real move gets a real reply, and that's where you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This isn't licence to ignore others. Hard-to-reverse moves, or ones that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first. Most moves are reversible, and for those the default is to make them openly.
- Example: instead of asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what changed and why, and invite reversal.

**7. Failures come in pairs.** Correcting one failure tends to push toward its mirror image. The pairs, as I recall them:
- inflating a claim / deflating it;
- inventing a flaw to look rigorous / inventing a reassurance to keep things moving;
- closing too early / keeping open too long;
- killing a live line at the first difficulty / keeping a dead one the evidence has ruled out;
- deferring (accepting a claim because of who made it) / dismissing (rejecting it for the same reason);
- offloading (asking others to decide what you can see) / overriding (deciding what genuinely needs others' input).

If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other. I'm fairly confident there were six pairs, but not certain of the order.

**A last word**
- It's not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those; they're how you find out what you didn't already know.

**Where I'm least certain:** exact wording throughout, whether §5 had an example, the order of the §7 pairs, and whether §6's list of visible moves had three items or more. If any of this will be quoted or relied on, check it against the text. By the note's own standard, my recollection isn't the referee.
